notes: A free light chain ratio over 100 is a defining characteristic of multiple myeloma.

End-organ damage (CRAB) means: hypercalcemia (serum calcium >11 mg/dL), renal insufficiency (creatinine clearance <40 mL/min or creatinine >2 mg/dL), anemia (hemoglobin <10 g/dL, or >2 g/dL below normal), and bone lesions (one or more osteolytic lesions ≥5 mm on skeletal radiography, MRI, CT or PET/CT). To count as diagnostic criteria, these changes must be attributable to the underlying plasma cell disorder.
Creatinine clearance is preferred over serum creatinine, because normal creatinine varies with age, sex and race.
Raised FDG uptake on PET, osteoporosis, or a vertebral compression fracture are not sufficient markers of bone lesions on their own. Where the diagnosis is in doubt, biopsy the bone lesion.
Non-CRAB end-organ damage — hyperviscosity syndrome, recurrent bacterial infection, AL amyloidosis, peripheral neuropathy — is nonspecific and not diagnostic of myeloma.

Biomarkers of near-inevitable progression (SLiM): ≥60% clonal plasma cells in the marrow; an involved/uninvolved free light chain ratio of 100 or more (with involved FLC at least 100 mg/L); or MRI showing more than one focal lesion.

notes: Wells score components, one point each: paralysis, paresis or recent orthopedic casting of a lower extremity; recently bedridden more than 3 days, or major surgery within the past 4 weeks; localized tenderness in the deep vein system; swelling of an entire leg; calf swelling 3 cm greater than the other leg, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity; pitting edema greater in the symptomatic leg; collateral nonvaricose superficial veins; active cancer, or cancer treated within the past 6 months. Minus two points if an alternative diagnosis is more likely than DVT.

Alternative diagnoses to consider: erysipelas, cellulitis, compartment syndrome, hypervolemia, Baker's cyst, muscle damage, postphlebitic syndrome, inguinal lymphadenopathy, external venous compression.
Provoked vs unprovoked: an unprovoked DVT implies no preventable action or environmental change would have prevented it. A provoked DVT has a clear trigger — surgery, trauma, immobilization.
Unprovoked DVT or PE warrants a hypercoagulability workup in certain populations: under 45, family history, recurrent or arterial thrombosis, or warfarin-induced skin necrosis.
